query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the alloy’s capacity to form and maintain a dynamically refined, ultra‐nanocrystalline (or amorphous) surface layer that fosters a robust, self-healing passive oxide film. This dual protective mechanism minimizes material loss from mechanical abrasion while maintaining chemical passivation.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed (e.g., as-cast or coarse-grained) high-entropy alloy such as an AlCoCrFeNiMo variant lacking deliberate microstructure refinement.
generation.intervention: Either alloy compositional tuning (e.g., doping with microalloying elements like B that promote in situ precipitation of fine reinforcing phases) or a controlled wear process to induce near-surface dynamic amorphization that refines the grain structure.
generation.conditions: Simultaneous wear and corrosion testing in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled sliding contact (tribocorrosion environment) at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-fine or amorphous near-surface layer that supports the rapid in situ development and repair of a protective passive oxide film.
generation.mechanism: During mechanical contact, the high shear forces induce grain refinement and even local amorphization at the surface. In parallel, the alloying elements (for example, Mo from the composition and possible additions like B driving fine-phase formation) promote the formation of a chemically stable passive layer. This self-renewing, refined layer diminishes both abrasive wear and corrosive degradation by ensuring that any disruption of the passivation is rapidly healed.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to a baseline alloy with a conventional, coarser surface microstructure, the alloy exhibiting the refined/amorphous surface will show a lower wear rate, reduced corrosion current density, and smaller shifts in open-circuit potential under tribocorrosion testing. In effect, the combined degradation (tribocorrosion) performance will be significantly better than that of the baseline due to the synergistic interaction between mechanical accommodation and chemical passivation.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy lacking either the induced nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer or the compositional modifications that promote its formation.
generation.boundary: This benefit is expected to hold under moderate operational temperatures and strain rates where the passive film remains stable. In environments with extreme temperatures or very high strain rates that disrupt the passive film faster than it can re-establish, the improved performance may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds for the critical grain size or amorphous fraction necessary for optimal protection remain uncertain. Moreover, the precise contributions of specific alloying elements (e.g., the level of Mo or B) to the stability and regeneration of the passive layer under varying environmental conditions need further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one processed to induce a refined/amorphous near-surface layer (via compositional tuning such as adding B or controlled sliding pre-treatment) and a baseline set with conventional processing. Expose both sets to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion testing in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under identical load, temperature, and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N-m) determined from wear track volume loss
Electrochemical measurements including corrosion current density and open-circuit potential (OCP) shifts
Surface microstructure characterization (using SEM/TEM) before and after testing to assess grain refinement and passive film integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower wear rate, lower corrosion current density, and more stable OCP) compared to the baseline, or if surface analysis fails to show evidence of a dynamically refined/amorphous passivating layer, then the proposed mechanism of synergistic protection via dynamic amorphization and passivation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe aim of the paper is to study the Zr addition effect on the mechanical properties and corrosion behavior of a high-entropy alloy from the CoCrFeMoNi system. This alloy was designed to be used for components in the geothermal industry that are exposed to high temperature and corrosion. Two alloys, one Zr-free (named Sample 1) and another one doped with 0.71 wt.% Zr (named Sample 2), were obtained in a vacuum arc remelting equipment from high-purity granular raw materials. Microstructural characterization and quantitative analysis by SEM and EDS were performed. The Young modulus values for the experimental alloys were calculated on the basis of a three-point bending test. Corrosion behavior was estimated by linear polarization test and by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The addition of Zr resulted in a decrease in the value of the Young modulus but also in a decrease in corrosion resistance. The beneficial effect of Zr on the microstructure was the grain refinement, and this ensured a good deoxidation of the alloy.Keywords: HEA, CoCrFeMoNiZr, microstructure, corrosion, EIS, Young modulus

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
